slides: Open by framing regular polygons as both circle divisions and finite symmetry machines. The same vertices can be studied arithmetically through constructibility, algebraically through roots of unity, geometrically through reflections, and dynamically through orbits such as kaleidoscopes and star polygons.

Use this route slide to keep the chapter coherent. The first half asks which circle divisions Euclidean tools can build, while the second half asks how rotations and reflections organize the resulting vertices. The star-polygon lab then shows number theory inside a cyclic orbit.

Cyclotomy turns regular polygons into roots of unity. The Gauss-Wantzel criterion filters constructible orders by powers of two and distinct Fermat primes. The slide should emphasize that this is not a drawing recipe; it is an arithmetic test for which divisions can be constructed.

The trisection slide gives the boundary case. Arbitrary angle trisection asks for a cubic whose degree is three in the sixty degree example, while straightedge-and-compass constructions can only build through repeated quadratic extensions. The obstruction is algebraic, not a failure of drawing skill.

The fixed-point isometry slide explains why reflections are so constrained. If two points are fixed, a third point must preserve both distances to them, leaving only the original point or its mirror across the fixed line. More fixed information leaves very little freedom.

The dihedral group slide converts the symmetry picture into algebra. A regular pentagon has five rotations and five reflections, the rotation has order five, the reflection squares to the identity, and conjugating a rotation by a reflection reverses it. That is the group in one diagram.

The product of reflections is the chapter's most productive mechanism. Two mirrors through the same point produce a rotation whose angle is twice the angle between the mirrors. Reversing the order gives the inverse rotation, so noncommutativity becomes visible as a geometric effect.

The kaleidoscope slide makes the dihedral group physical. Two mirrors at angle pi over n generate two n visible images, half preserving orientation and half reversing it. The static figure uses n equals seven, and the companion HTML lets students vary the wedge.

Star polygons show how the same cyclic orbit can draw different geometry. When p and q are coprime, the step q visits all p vertices; when the greatest common divisor is larger, the path splits into cycles. The density and area checks certify the drawing.

Close by linking the arithmetic and symmetry halves of the chapter. Constructibility filters which regular polygons Euclidean tools can make, while cyclic and dihedral actions explain how their vertices move. The chapter's checks keep the algebra, figures, and orbit tables aligned.
